# Book III, Proposition 24

*Similar segments on equal straight lines are equal*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> Similar segments of circles on equal straight lines are equal to one another.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved in part: equal circles and measures; the segments stay in Euclid's words · a different argument

<p align="center"><em>Lay the segment AEB on CFD, A on C and B on D: with equal bases AB, CD (blue) and equal angles AEB, CFD in them (yellow), the two fit exactly, and are equal (red).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/24.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition III.24, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For let AEB, CFD be similar segments of circles on equal straight lines AB, CD;

I say that the segment AEB is equal to the segment CFD.

For, if the segment AEB be applied to CFD, and if the point A be placed on C and the straight line AB on CD,

the point B will also coincide with the point D, because AB is equal to CD;

and, AB coinciding with CD,

the segment AEB will also coincide with CFD.

For, if the straight line AB coincide with CD but the segment AEB do not coincide with CFD,

it will either fall within it, or outside it;

or it will fall awry, as CGD, and a circle cuts a circle at more points than two: which is impossible. [III. 10]

Therefore, if the straight line AB be applied to CD, the segment AEB will not fail to coincide with CFD also;

therefore it will coincide with it and will be equal to it.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

| Proof | ✅ Proved |
| Statement | In part. Proves the circles equal and the circumferences equal in the angle measure; that the segments are equal, one laid on the other, is left to the text. |
| Argument | A different argument. Euclid applies one segment to the other. The Lean moves no figure, for superposition belongs to I.4 and I.8 alone, and compares the radii instead, by the angles at the centres (III.20, III.22) and isosceles triangles on the equal bases (`Prop24.isosceles`). |
| Representation | Equal segments are read as equal circles with equal measures of their circumferences, each circle coming with a centre. The measure carries no radius, so the second clause follows from the equal angles at E and F alone; the equal bases are needed for the first. |

Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out. **How the Lean follows the text**

- **Argued another way.** "For, if the segment AEB be applied to CFD…" In place of applying the segment, the Lean compares the circles by their radii: the equal angles at E and F place the centres alike (`Prop24.angle_type`), and equal angles at the centres on equal bases give equal radii.
- **Argued another way.** "For, if the straight line AB coincide with CD…" With the radii already equal, no segment is left to fall within, outside or awry, so the Lean refutes none of the three and cites neither III.10 nor III.23.
- **Argued another way.** "therefore it will coincide with it and will be equal to it." The circumferences are equal by the measure: each, with the circumference on the other side of its base, which is twice the equal angle at E or F, makes up the whole circle (`Circumference.whole`).

```lean
/-- The halves of unequal things are unequal, the less to the less: if `a` and `a` together
are less than `b` and `b` together, then `a` is less than `b`. Were `a` equal to `b`, or
greater, the doubles would be equal, or the greater. -/
theorem Prop24.half_lt {k : Kind} {a b : Magnitude k} (h : a + a < b + b) : a < b := by
  rcases lt_trichotomy a b with h' | h' | h'
  · exact h'
  · subst h'; exact absurd h (lt_irrefl _)
  · exact absurd (lt_trans h (Magnitude.add_self_lt_add_self h')) (lt_irrefl _)

/-- The angle in a segment is acute, right or obtuse as the centre lies on its side of
the base, on the base, or beyond it. -/
theorem Prop24.angle_type {X Y Z M : Point} {α : Circle} (hM : Centre M α) (hX : OnCircle X α)
    (hY : OnCircle Y α) (hZ : OnCircle Z α) (hXYZ : Triangle X Y Z) :
    (SameSideOf M Z X Y ∧ ∠ X Z Y < ∟) ∨ (Between X M Y ∧ ∠ X Z Y = ∟) ∨
      (OppositeSidesOf M Z X Y ∧ ∟ < ∠ X Z Y) := by
  obtain ⟨W, hW, hWZ⟩ := Prop2.oppositeSide ⟨M, hM⟩ hX hY hXYZ
  have hm : circumference α X W Y = ∠ X Z Y + ∠ X Z Y := Circumference.eq ⟨M, hM⟩ hZ hX hY hWZ.symm
  obtain ⟨L, hX_L, hY_L⟩ := Postulate1 X Y hXYZ.ne₁₂
  by_cases hM_L : OnLine M L
  · have hXMY := between_of_inside_chord hM_L hX_L hY_L (centre_inside hM) hX hY hXYZ.ne₁₂
    have hs := Circumference.semicircle hM hX hY hXMY hWZ.triangle
    rw [hm] at hs
    exact Or.inr (Or.inl ⟨hXMY, Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq hs⟩)
  by_cases hs : SameSide M Z L
  · have hMZ : SameSideOf M Z X Y := SameSideOf.of_line hXYZ.ne₁₂ hX_L hY_L hs
    have hlt := Circumference.lt_semicircle hM hX hY (hMZ.trans_opposite hWZ.symm)
    rw [hm] at hlt
    exact Or.inl ⟨hMZ, Prop24.half_lt hlt⟩
  · have hMZ : OppositeSidesOf M Z X Y :=
      OppositeSidesOf.of_line hXYZ.ne₁₂ hX_L hY_L ⟨hM_L, hXYZ.off_line hX_L hY_L, hs⟩
    have hgt := Circumference.gt_semicircle hM hX hY (OppositeSidesOf.sameSideOf hMZ.symm hWZ.symm)
    rw [hm] at hgt
    exact Or.inr (Or.inr ⟨hMZ, Prop24.half_lt hgt⟩)

/-- Isosceles triangles on equal bases with equal angles at the vertex have equal sides. The
angles at the base are equal by I.5, the three angles make two right angles by I.32, and two
angles and the side between them give the equal sides by I.26. -/
theorem Prop24.isosceles {A B G C D H : Point} (hABG : Triangle A B G) (hCDH : Triangle C D H)
    (hG : ‖G A‖ = ‖G B‖) (hH : ‖H C‖ = ‖H D‖) (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖)
    (hang : ∠ A G B = ∠ C H D) : ‖G A‖ = ‖H C‖ := by
  have b₁ : ∠ G A B = ∠ G B A := BookI.Prop5.base hABG.cab hG
  have b₂ : ∠ H C D = ∠ H D C := BookI.Prop5.base hCDH.cab hH
  obtain ⟨P, hBGP⟩ := produce hABG.ne₂₃
  obtain ⟨-, s₁⟩ := BookI.Prop32 hABG hBGP
  obtain ⟨Q, hDHQ⟩ := produce hCDH.ne₂₃
  obtain ⟨-, s₂⟩ := BookI.Prop32 hCDH hDHQ
  have t₁ : ∠ G A B + ∠ G A B + ∠ A G B = ∟ + ∟ := by
    rw [← s₁, angle_symm hABG.ne₁₂ hABG.ne₂₃.symm, ← b₁, angle_symm hABG.ne₂₃ hABG.ne₁₃]
    ac_rfl
  have t₂ : ∠ H C D + ∠ H C D + ∠ C H D = ∟ + ∟ := by
    rw [← s₂, angle_symm hCDH.ne₁₂ hCDH.ne₂₃.symm, ← b₂, angle_symm hCDH.ne₂₃ hCDH.ne₁₃]
    ac_rfl
  have hA : ∠ G A B = ∠ H C D :=
    Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq (CommonNotion3 (by rw [t₁, t₂]) hang)
  have hB : ∠ A B G = ∠ C D H := by
    rw [angle_symm hABG.ne₁₂ hABG.ne₂₃.symm, ← b₁, hA, b₂, angle_symm hCDH.ne₂₃.symm hCDH.ne₁₂]
  exact (BookI.Prop26 hABG.cab hCDH.cab hA hB (Or.inl hAB)).1
```

```lean
/-- Similar segments of circles on equal straight lines are equal to one another. -/
theorem Prop24 {A B C D E F : Point} {AEB CFD : Circle} (hAEB : ∃ O : Point, Centre O AEB)
    (hCFD : ∃ O : Point, Centre O CFD) (hA : OnCircle A AEB) (hB : OnCircle B AEB)
    (hE : OnCircle E AEB) (hC : OnCircle C CFD) (hD : OnCircle D CFD)
    (hF : OnCircle F CFD) (hE_AB : ¬ Collinear A B E) (hF_CD : ¬ Collinear C D F)
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖C D‖) (hsim : ∠ A E B = ∠ C F D) :
    EqualCircles AEB CFD ∧ circumference AEB A E B = circumference CFD C F D := by
  -- For let AEB, CFD be similar segments of circles on equal straight lines AB, CD;
  obtain ⟨M, hM⟩ := hAEB
  obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ := hCFD
  have hABE : Triangle A B E := hE_AB
  have hCDF : Triangle C D F := hF_CD
  obtain ⟨X, hX, hXE⟩ := Prop2.oppositeSide ⟨M, hM⟩ hA hB hABE
  obtain ⟨Y, hY, hYF⟩ := Prop2.oppositeSide ⟨N, hN⟩ hC hD hCDF
  -- I say that the segment AEB is equal to the segment CFD.
  -- For, if the segment AEB be applied to CFD, and if the point A be placed on C and the
  -- straight line AB on CD,
  /- In place of applying the segment, we compare the circles by their radii MA, NC, from
     the centres M, N. -/
  have hMA : ‖M A‖ = ‖M B‖ := Definition15 hM hA hB
  have hNC : ‖N C‖ = ‖N D‖ := Definition15 hN hC hD
  -- the point B will also coincide with the point D, because AB is equal to CD;
  /- On the equal bases AB, CD, equal angles at the centres make the radii equal, by III.20
     and `Prop24.isosceles`; and so do two diameters, each the double of a radius. -/
  have central : ∀ {P Q : Point}, OnCircle P AEB → OnCircle Q CFD → SameSideOf M P A B →
      SameSideOf N Q C D → ∠ A P B = ∠ C Q D → ‖M A‖ = ‖N C‖ := by
    intro P Q hP hQ hMP hNQ hPQ
    exact Prop24.isosceles hMP.triangle hNQ.triangle hMA hNC hAB (by
      rw [Prop20 hM hP hA hB hMP, Prop20 hN hQ hC hD hNQ, hPQ])
  have diam : Between A M B → Between C N D → ‖M A‖ = ‖N C‖ := by
    intro hAMB hCND
    have d₁ : ‖A B‖ = ‖M A‖ + ‖M A‖ := by
      rw [← len_add_of_between hAMB, len_symm A M, ← hMA]
    have d₂ : ‖C D‖ = ‖N C‖ + ‖N C‖ := by
      rw [← len_add_of_between hCND, len_symm C N, ← hNC]
    exact Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq (d₁.symm.trans (hAB.trans d₂))
  -- and, AB coinciding with CD,
  /- The segments on the other sides of AB, CD, at X and Y, are similar too: the angle in
     each makes two right angles with the angle at E or F [III. 22]. -/
  have q₁ : ∠ A E B + ∠ A X B = ∟ + ∟ := by
    have := (Prop22 ⟨M, hM⟩ hE hA hX hB hXE.symm).2
    rwa [angle_symm hXE.triangle.ne₂₃ hXE.triangle.ne₁₃] at this
  have q₂ : ∠ C F D + ∠ C Y D = ∟ + ∟ := by
    have := (Prop22 ⟨N, hN⟩ hF hC hY hD hYF.symm).2
    rwa [angle_symm hYF.triangle.ne₂₃ hYF.triangle.ne₁₃] at this
  have hXY : ∠ A X B = ∠ C Y D := by
    apply CommonNotion3 (c := ∠ A E B) (d := ∠ C F D) _ hsim
    rw [add_comm (∠ A X B), q₁, add_comm (∠ C Y D), q₂]
  -- the segment AEB will also coincide with CFD.
  /- The circles are equal. The equal angles at E, F are both less than a right angle,
     both right, or both greater, so the centres lie alike: on the sides of E and F, on the
     bases, or beyond them, where X and Y serve. -/
  have hrad : ‖M A‖ = ‖N C‖ := by
    rcases Prop24.angle_type hM hA hB hE hABE with ⟨hME, hlt⟩ | ⟨hAMB, hrt⟩ | ⟨hME, hgt⟩ <;>
      rcases Prop24.angle_type hN hC hD hF hCDF with ⟨hNF, hlt'⟩ | ⟨hCND, hrt'⟩ | ⟨hNF, hgt'⟩
    · exact central hE hF hME hNF hsim
    · rw [hsim, hrt'] at hlt; exact absurd hlt (lt_irrefl _)
    · rw [hsim] at hlt; exact absurd (lt_trans hlt hgt') (lt_irrefl _)
    · rw [← hsim, hrt] at hlt'; exact absurd hlt' (lt_irrefl _)
    · exact diam hAMB hCND
    · rw [← hsim, hrt] at hgt'; exact absurd hgt' (lt_irrefl _)
    · rw [hsim] at hgt; exact absurd (lt_trans hlt' hgt) (lt_irrefl _)
    · rw [hsim, hrt'] at hgt; exact absurd hgt (lt_irrefl _)
    · exact central hX hY (OppositeSidesOf.sameSideOf hME.symm hXE.symm)
        (OppositeSidesOf.sameSideOf hNF.symm hYF.symm) hXY
  -- For, if the straight line AB coincide with CD but the segment AEB do not coincide with
  -- CFD,
  -- it will either fall within it, or outside it;
  -- or it will fall awry, as CGD, and a circle cuts a circle at more points than two: which is
  -- impossible. [III. 10]
  /- The radii are already equal, by the angles at the centres, so nothing is left for
     III.10 to refute. -/
  -- Therefore, if the straight line AB be applied to CD, the segment AEB will not fail to
  -- coincide with CFD also;
  refine ⟨⟨M, N, A, C, hM, hN, hA, hC, hrad⟩, ?_⟩
  -- therefore it will coincide with it and will be equal to it.
  /- Each circumference, with the one on the other side of its base, which is twice the
     angle at E or F, makes up the whole circle; so the remainders are equal [C.N. 3]. -/
  have w₁ := Circumference.whole ⟨M, hM⟩ hA hB hXE
  have w₂ := Circumference.whole ⟨N, hN⟩ hC hD hYF
  rw [Circumference.eq ⟨M, hM⟩ hE hA hB hXE.symm] at w₁
  rw [Circumference.eq ⟨N, hN⟩ hF hC hD hYF.symm, ← hsim] at w₂
  exact CommonNotion3 (w₁.trans w₂.symm) rfl
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

- [`pasch2`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L70) (through [`Circumference.eq`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L49), [`Circumference.gt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L163), [`Circumference.lt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L148) and 4 other lemmas): If B is between A and C, A is on L and B is off it, then B and C are on the same side of L: a straight line that leaves L at A does not cross it again. (Pasch 2)
- [`same_side_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L63) (through [`Circumference.eq`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L49), [`Circumference.gt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L163), [`Circumference.lt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L148) and 6 other lemmas): Two points on the same side of a straight line as a third point are on the same side as each other. (Same side 4)

**Lengths, angles and areas**

- [`angle_add_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L47) (through [`Circumference.eq`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L49), [`Circumference.gt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L163), [`Circumference.lt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L148) and 4 other lemmas): If D lies within the angle BAC, then BAC is made up of BAD and DAC. (Diagram-angle 2)
- [`angle_eq_of_same_rays`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L54) (through [`Circumference.semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L107)): The angle doesn't change if its arms are traced through other points on the same rays. (Diagram-angle 4)
- [`angle_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L27) (used here): The angle ABC is the angle CBA. (Metric 4)
- [`area_add_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L70): Cutting a triangle in two from a vertex adds up. (Diagram-area 2)
- [`area_congruent`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L41): Triangles equal in all their sides and angles are equal in area. Euclid uses this without comment once he has shown two triangles congruent. (Metric 9)
- [`area_degenerate`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L33): A "triangle" with a repeated corner has no area. (Metric 6)
- [`area_eq_zero_of_on_line`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L62): A "triangle" whose corners lie on one straight line has no area. (Diagram-area 1)
- [`area_rotate`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L36): The triangle ABC is the triangle CAB. (Metric 8)
- [`circle_eq`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L30) (through [`Circumference.eq`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L49), [`Circumference.gt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L163), [`Circumference.lt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L148) and 6 other lemmas): A circle is fixed by its centre and its radius. (Diagram-segment 2)
- [`len_add_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L27) (used here): If B is between A and C, then AB and BC together make up AC. (Diagram-segment 1)
- [`len_self`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L21) (through [`Circumference.eq`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L49), [`Circumference.gt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L163), [`Circumference.lt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L148) and 6 other lemmas): The "straight line" from a point to itself has no length. (Metric 1)
- [`len_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L24) (used here): The straight line AB is the straight line BA. (Metric 3)
- [`same_ray_of_angle_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L42) (through [`Circumference.eq`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L49), [`Circumference.gt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L163), [`Circumference.lt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L148) and 4 other lemmas): If the angle BAC is nothing, C lies on the ray from A through B. (Diagram-angle 1)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L48): **Superposition.** A hypothetical placement of a triangle on a given ray and side permits a restricted derivation of metric equalities about the figure already given. The derivation introduces no further objects, cites each geometric law it uses, and exports no symbol of the placement.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_assoc`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L23) (through [`Circumference.gt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L163), [`Circumference.lt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L148), [`Circumference.semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L107) and 3 other lemmas): Adding three magnitudes in a row, it makes no difference whether the first two or the last two are added first. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L26) (used here): The order of adding does not matter. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L45) (through [`Circumference.eq`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L49), [`Circumference.gt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L163), [`Circumference.lt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L148) and 4 other lemmas): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L29): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L32) (used here): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L35) (used here): What is less than the less is less still. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L39) (used here): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L42) (through [`Circumference.eq`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L49), [`Circumference.gt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L163), [`Circumference.lt_semicircle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean#L148) and 6 other lemmas): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

</details>

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

**"If the segment AEB be applied to CFD."** Euclid lays the segment AEB on CFD, A on C and AB along CD. The equal bases bring B onto D, and the equal angles in the segments must then bring the circumferences together. Superposition is a method Euclid uses as little as he can, Heath remarks in his note on Definition III.1, and here he needs it. Our statement says less: the circles AEB, CFD are equal, and the circumferences AEB, CFD are equal in our measure, twice the angle that stands on each. It does not say that one segment can be laid on the other. Since the measure carries no radius, the equal angles alone give the equal circumferences; it is the equal circles that take work.

**Within, outside, or across?** If the bases fit and the segments do not, the one falls within the other, outside it, or across it. Heath puts a semicolon after "outside it", where the Greek has a comma, so that III.10 answers only the third: "The first two hypotheses are disposed of by a *tacit* reference to the preceding proposition III. 23" (vol. 2, p. 54). Robert Simson's version says no more than that: once AB lies on CD, the segments fit by III.23, as Heath reports under that proposition.

**"Fall awry."** It is the word of I.8, Heath notes: "The word implies that the applied figure will partly fall short of, and partly overlap, the figure to which it is applied" (vol. 2, p. 54). The thin curve CGD, Heath's as well, is that impossible case: it meets CFD at C, at D and once more, and a circle does not cut a circle at more points than two (III.10).

**Equal radii without moving the segments.** Our rules lay no segment on another, superposition being kept for I.4 and I.8, so we compare the circles by their radii instead. The angle in a segment tells where the centre lies, so the equal angles at E and F place both centres alike, and III.20 and III.22 then give equal angles at the centres, on equal bases, and so equal radii. Euclid needs III.10 to rule out a segment that falls awry; with the radii equal first, we never do.

**The modern way.** A segment on a straight line of length c, with the angle θ in it, lies in a circle of radius c/(2 sin θ), by the law of sines, and its arc subtends 2π − 2θ at the centre, so equal c and θ give equal radii and equal arcs. It is not Euclid's route: he lays one segment on the other.

## Further reading

- For the radius c/(2 sin θ) of the modern way, the extended law of sines, Evan Chen's [*Euclidean Geometry in Mathematical Olympiads*](https://doi.org/10.5948/9781614444114) (2016), §3.1, "The Extended Law of Sines" (p. 43), written for olympiad students and more demanding than most books here, but a lively modern course in Book III's ideas.
- For what Hippocrates of Chios did with similar segments, which are to one another as the squares on their bases, and the first lune he squared with them, J. J. O'Connor and E. F. Robertson's ["Hippocrates of Chios"](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Hippocrates/) (free online), a short, clear page on the first geometer known to have written *Elements*, which draws that lune, on a right-angled isosceles triangle in a semicircle, for you to follow.
